titre: The US Federal Minimum Wage Failed First, Then Held
accroche: In 1933, Washington imposes a federal minimum wage through economic codes. The Supreme Court strikes it down in 1935. A second law, in 1938, finally holds.
contenu_vulgarise:
In June 1933, at the height of the New Deal, Congress passes the National Industrial Recovery Act (NIRA). The law authorizes industry codes, negotiated among manufacturers, that set minimum wages and maximum working hours in each sector. Several hundred codes are adopted within a year, from steel to textiles.

## A Law Struck Down for Overreach

On May 27, 1935, the US Supreme Court, in *Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States*, unanimously declares the NIRA unconstitutional. The case concerns the live poultry code, which the Schechter company, a Brooklyn slaughterhouse run by four brothers, is accused of violating. The Court rules that Congress delegated far too broad a regulatory power to the executive, and that the trade covered by this code, ordinary local slaughterhouses whose poultry does not travel on to another state, is not closely enough tied to interstate commerce to fall within its constitutional authority. The NIRA codes, minimum wage included, cease to apply overnight.

## A Second Law, Narrower and Better Targeted

Secretary of Labor Frances Perkins has to find another way. On June 25, 1938, Franklin Roosevelt signs the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), which this time sets directly, through the statute itself rather than delegated codes, a minimum wage of twenty-five cents an hour, a working-hours threshold beyond which overtime is paid at one and a half times the rate, and bans on the employment of children under sixteen in manufacturing and mining. The text covers only employees whose work falls within interstate commerce, so as to rest more narrowly on the same constitutional clause the Court had just invoked against the NIRA.

## The Second Test, and the Reversal of an 1918 Precedent

Fred Darby, the owner of a lumber mill in Statesboro, Georgia, keeps paying his workers below the minimum set by the 1938 law. Prosecuted, he first wins on appeal, a judge ruling that the Tenth Amendment reserved the regulation of so local an activity to the states. On February 3, 1941, the Supreme Court, in *United States v. Darby Lumber Co.*, unanimously reverses that decision. It rules that Congress's power over interstate commerce does not depend on whether the states exercise their own powers, and to write this it sets aside the distinction between manufacturing and commerce that the same Court had drawn in 1918, in *Hammer v. Dagenhart*, to strike down an earlier federal law on child labor.

Between 1933 and 1941, the same constitutional question, that of the limit of federal power over labor, receives two opposite answers: good legislative intent was not enough to make a rule hold; it took a second law, written narrowly enough, to pass the test that had brought down the first.

repere.texte: The decision in *United States v. Darby Lumber Co.*, handed down unanimously on February 3, 1941, explicitly overturns the 1918 decision in *Hammer v. Dagenhart*, by which the Supreme Court had struck down the first federal law on child labor.
repere.source: Supreme Court of the United States, United States v. Darby Lumber Co., 312 U.S. 100 (1941)

carte.punch: The US federal minimum wage failed at first, then held on its second law.
carte.idee: In 1933, a federal minimum wage set by economic codes is struck down by the Supreme Court in 1935, for overreach. It takes a second law, the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, passed by Congress, for the Court to uphold it in 1941, by reversing an 1918 precedent.

quiz.question: Why did the first American attempt at a federal minimum wage, set through the codes of the National Industrial Recovery Act, fail in 1935?
choix: Because Congress had never passed a law authorizing these codes
Because the Court ruled the power delegated to the executive too broad, and the activity too local for interstate commerce
Because manufacturers had refused to apply the codes as soon as they were adopted
Because President Roosevelt had withdrawn the National Industrial Recovery Act himself
quiz.explication: The Supreme Court, in Schechter Poultry (1935), ruled the delegation of power to the executive unconstitutional and the targeted activity too local to fall under the commerce clause. Congress had indeed passed the law in 1933, manufacturers were applying it, and Roosevelt did not withdraw the statute himself: it was the Court that struck it down.
